content.text:
Let me judge rows 16-46.

Row 16 (n=58): "my daughter picked the colours: she wants Family in violet. Can you do that?"
sop: c1 declarative picked; c2 declarative wants; k1 coordination (no conjunction) c1 c2; r1 marker=in from n4(Family) to n5(violet); c3 interrogative Can do subject you complement that.
"Can you do that?" is a question - interrogative with auxiliary Can, verb do, subject you. Good.
"Family in violet" — r1 from n4 to n5: fine.
c2 complement=n4 only; "violet" tied by r1. Fine.
Accept L8.

Row 17 (n=59): "the red on the Work calendar feels alarming - could we go with a calm navy?"
sop: n1 "the red"; r1 marker on from n1 to n2; c1 declarative feels modifier alarming subject n1; c2 interrogative could go subject we; r2 with from c2 to n4; r3 from c2 to c1.
Fine. "alarming" as modifier — per settled case "the red ... feels alarming" adjective after verb → modifier. Good. L8.

Row 18 (n=60): "Family a bit darker"
sop: c1 imperative verb=Family modifier=darker complement=n1("a bit" head bit, dep a).
Issues: "Family" as a verb (a noun made verb) → L1 per settled case ("A noun made its verb is L1"; "A command needs its verb. When the first word ... can be a noun or a verb ... it is the verb; held as a noun in a fragment, the command is lost: L1"). Hmm, but here "Family" is not plausibly a verb. The message "Family a bit darker" has no verb at all: fragment. Its verb is written as "Family" — a noun made the verb of an imperative clause. That's clearly L1: "A message or a part with no verb ('pie radius smaller', 'legend on the right', 'a fireplace') is a fragment. Its nominals that are not the end of a relation are its complement. A noun made its verb is L1."

Also "a bit darker": per settled case, "A word that grades a graded word ('a bit longer'...) are modifier words of the clause, as one run or word by word; 'a bit' or 'a little' may also stand as a nominal of its own (a measure)." So n1 "a bit" is fine (measure nominal). But is n1 tied? It's a complement of c1 → it's in a wire (complement), so not untied (it's not "tied to nothing" since it's a complement). OK.

Main error: verb "Family" → L1. Quote: 'Family a bit darker'. Correction: fragment with complement "Family" and modifiers "a" "bit" "darker" (or a bit nominal + darker modifier).

Correction:
@n1 syntax.nominal head="Family"
@n2 syntax.nominal dependent="a" head="bit"
@c1 syntax.clause form=fragment modifier="darker" complement=$n1 complement=$n2

Hmm, is "a bit" as a nominal complement fine? The case says "a bit" may stand as a nominal of its own (a measure). Yes. But a fragment's complement should be its nominals — fine.

Alternatively simpler: @c1 fragment modifier="a" modifier="bit" modifier="darker" complement=$n1. Both pass. I'll use the first.

Row 19 (n=62): "colour it gold" — sop: fragment with three nominals as complements. "colour" is a verb here (imperative). Held as a noun in a fragment → the command is lost → L1. Correction:
@c1 syntax.clause form=imperative verb="colour" modifier="gold" complement=$n1
@n1 syntax.nominal head="it"

Row 20 (n=63): "gym calendar: something brighter"
sop: n1 gym calendar; n2 "something"; c1 fragment modifier=brighter complement=n2; c2 fragment complement=n1; k1 coordination conjunct c2 c1.
Both parts verbless → fragments. Fine. "something brighter": head "something" with "brighter" as modifier of the clause — per settled case "font bigger" → modifier of clause. Good. L8.

Row 21 (n=66): "please get rid of the Work calendar"
sop: c1 imperative discourse=please auxiliary="get" verb="rid"; r1 marker=of from c1 to n1.
Hmm: "get rid of" — "get" as auxiliary and "rid" as verb. Is "get" an auxiliary? "get rid of X" — "get" is the main verb, "rid" a participle/adjective. Writing auxiliary="get" verb="rid" — is that wrong? L1: "Its verb is a word that is no verb here, or an auxiliary while the main verb stands elsewhere." Hmm, "rid" as verb — "rid" is arguably the verb (to rid). "get rid of" is a fixed phrase. The alt for row 28 similar. I think acceptable: "get" auxiliary-ish (causative-ish), "rid" the verb. The next layer can continue. Also "of" marker, fine. L8? I lean accept — the words are all placed, verb identified. Hmm, but "get" as auxiliary — "get" is not an auxiliary in "get rid of". L1 says "Its verb is a word that is no verb here, or an auxiliary while the main verb stands elsewhere". Here the verb is "rid" (a verb-ish word) and the auxiliary is "get". Is "get" an auxiliary while the main verb stands elsewhere? The main verb (get) stands at the auxiliary slot, and "rid" is written as the verb. So the error would be "an auxiliary while the main verb stands elsewhere" — i.e., writing the auxiliary "get" where the main verb is "rid"... no: this rule describes writing as `verb` an auxiliary word while the main verb is elsewhere. Here verb="rid" — is "rid" an auxiliary? No. So the rule's target isn't matched.

I'll accept: it identifies the verb phrase "get rid", verb "rid", and "of the Work calendar" related. Fine, L8.

Row 22 (n=68): "I want the Gym calendar gone"
sop: c1 declarative want subject I; n2 "the Gym calendar"; c2 nonfinite verb=gone subject=n2; r1 c1→c2.
"gone" as a nonfinite verb with subject "the Gym calendar". Subject of c2 — words show "the Gym calendar" is the object of want and the subject of "gone". Fine. Accept L8.

Row 23 (n=72): "I cancelled my membership, so the Gym calendar can go"
sop: c1 declarative cancelled subject I complement n2; r1 marker=so from c1 to c2?? Wait: "@r1 syntax.relation marker="so" from=$c1 to=$n2" — from c1 to n2 ("my membership")! That's wrong: "so" should link c1 and c2. The end n2 is "my membership".

Hmm, wait, r1: marker "so" from=c1 to=n2. n2 = "my membership". So the relation marked "so" ends at "my membership" — but "so" stands before "the Gym calendar can go". So the relation has the wrong end → L3. And c2 is then untied? c2 = "the Gym calendar can go" — is it an end of any relation? No other relation mentions c2. So c2 is a clause tied to nothing.

Hmm wait, but also c1 complies. So two faults: wrong end of relation (L3) and untied clause (L6). First grade: L3.

Hold on. Let me double check: maybe the sop intends "so" relation c1→n2 wrongly. Yes as printed: `@r1 syntax.relation marker="so" from=$c1 to=$n2`. n2 defined after: `@n2 syntax.nominal dependent="my" head="membership"`. Yes, wrong end.

So L3 for n=72. Quote: 'so the Gym calendar can go'. Correction: r1 from c1 to c2 marker="so".

Correction:
@n1 nominal head="I"
@c1 declarative verb="cancelled" subject=$n1 complement=$n2
@n2 nominal dependent="my" head="membership"
@n3 nominal dependent="the" dependent="Gym" head="calendar"
@c2 declarative auxiliary="can" verb="go" subject=$n3
@r1 relation marker="so" from=$c1 to=$c2

Row 24 (n=75): "rename Work to Office and then delete Gym altogether"
sop: c1 imperative rename complement n1(Work); r1 marker=to attachment=ambiguous from c1 to n2(Office); k1 and c1 c2; c2 imperative modifier=then verb=delete modifier=altogether complement=n3(Gym). Good. L8.

Row 25 (n=77): "honestly I never look at Travel anymore; would you mind deleting that calendar?"
sop: c1 declarative modifier=honestly negation=never verb=look modifier=anymore subject=I; r1 marker=at from c1 to n2(Travel); c2 interrogative aux=would verb=mind subject=you; c3 nonfinite verb=deleting complement=n4; k1 coordination c1 c2; r2 from c2 to c3.
"honestly" as modifier of the clause — allowed ("What a modifier says is not judged"; a word that is neither nominal nor marker). Fine. L8.

Row 26 (n=78): "no more Gym calendar" — fragment n1 head=calendar deps no, more, Gym. "no" as dependent — quantity phrase allowed. Fine. L8.

Row 27 (n=81): "lose the gym one" — c1 imperative verb=lose complement n1("the gym"); n2 "one"; r1 from n1 to n2. Hmm: "the gym one" — "one" as a separate nominal tied to n1. Is that fine? "the gym" nominal headed "gym" with dep "the", then "one" tied by relation without marker. Per settled case: "A number or a name right after a noun may be a dependent ... or a nominal of its own tied to the noun by a relation without a marker. Both pass." "one" is a pronoun, not a number/name. Is n2 "one" tied? Yes by r1. Not untied. Acceptable? The reading is a bit odd but not a wrong statement: "one" describes which thing. Hmm, the alternative would be one nominal "the gym one" with head "one" and "gym" dependent. Both readings are about the same thing. Accept L8.

Row 28 (n=83): "get rid of it, the calendar I just picked"
sop: c1 imperative aux=get verb=rid; r1 marker=of from c1 to n1(it); n2 "the calendar"; n3 I; c2 declarative modifier=just verb=picked subject=n3; r2 from n1 to n2; r3 from n2 to c2 ("the calendar I just picked" relative clause tied to n2). Good. L8.

Row 29 (n=86): "please add a new person, Jamal"
sop: c1 imperative please add complement n1; n2 Jamal; r1 from n1 to n2. Good (apposition tie). L8.

Row 30 (n=88): "put Dr. Hughes on the list of people"
sop: c1 imperative put complement n1 (Dr/Hughes); r1 marker=on attachment=ambiguous from c1 to n2(the list); r2 marker=of from n2 to n3(people). Good. L8.

Row 31 (n=90): "we've got a new designer starting Monday - please add Noor so I can invite her to things"
sop: c1 declarative aux='ve verb=got subject=we complement=n2; c2 nonfinite verb=starting complement=n3(Monday); c3 imperative please add complement=n4(Noor); r1 marker=so from c3 to c4; c4 declarative aux=can verb=invite subject=I complement=her; r2 marker=to from c4 to n7(things); r3 from c3 to c1; r4 from n2 to c2.

Hmm, r3: from c3 to c1 — a relation without marker between the command and the first clause (dash join). Fine-ish.
"starting Monday": c2 nonfinite verb=starting complement=Monday, tied to n2 (designer). Good.
Accept L8.

Row 32 (n=91): "add Ben as a person and then book him into the budget sync" — follows row 24 pattern. L8.

Row 33 (n=93): "so my brother is visiting next month; can you add him as Radu so I can put him on family events?"
sop: c1 declarative modifier=so aux=is verb=visiting subject=n1 complement=n2 ("next month" as complement); c2 interrogative can add subject you complement him; r1 marker=as from c2 to n5(Radu); r2 marker=so from c2 to c3; c3 declarative can put subject I complement him; r3 marker=on from c3 to n8(family events); k1 coordination c1 c2.
"so" at start as modifier: allowed per settled case (like "Now" at start may be discourse or modifier — for "so"? The settled case says "And/Then/So at the start of a message, with nothing before it to join, is a discourse word". Held as modifier of the clause: hmm, that's neither. Is "so" as modifier wrong? L2 is about content words in discourse; the reverse isn't listed. "Words stand in the wrong wire" (L3) — a modifier says manner/degree etc. "so" at the start of a message: is it losing information? Not much. Hmm, but here the risk: is it a wrong statement? It's a discourse/opening word held as a clause modifier. The rules explicitly permit discourse for it, and permit "Now" as modifier. I'd accept — a plausible reading the next layer can continue from.

Also "next month" as complement of c1 — fine (time phrase in the right clause; rules say a day/measure after a marker belongs to the clause; complement vs modifier isn't judged). L8.

Row 34 (n=99): "Hannah needs adding"
sop: n1 Hannah; c1 declarative auxiliary="needs" verb="adding" subject=n1.
Hmm: "needs adding" — "needs" is the main verb, "adding" a gerund. Writing "needs" as auxiliary and "adding" as verb: L1? "Its verb is a word that is no verb here, or an auxiliary while the main verb stands elsewhere." "needs" written as auxiliary while the main verb ("needs") stands... here the verb is "adding". "needs" is not an auxiliary; it's the main verb. So the circuit puts the main verb in the auxiliary slot and a gerund in the verb slot. Hmm, that's like row 8 ("keep getting": verb keep, then nonfinite clause with getting as aux, mixed as verb).

For "Hannah needs adding": there's one clause: subject Hannah, verb needs, complement "adding" (gerund). The sop writes: auxiliary=needs, verb=adding, single clause, declarative. Is that a wrong statement that must be undone? The next layer would read "needs" as an auxiliary and "adding" as the verb, i.e., a progressive-ish "is adding"? It loses that Hannah is the one who needs (needs is the main verb) — actually no: subject=Hannah applies to the clause; so it'd read "Hannah needs-aux adding" — roughly "Hannah is added"? That's wrong: Hannah is not the one adding nor being added... well "needs adding" = "needs to be added". The next layer reading "Hannah" as subject of "adding" gives "Hannah adds" — wrong direction (she's the one to be added).

Is that L1 ("an auxiliary while the main verb stands elsewhere")? The wording: writing as `verb` a word that is no verb here, or writing as `auxiliary`... hmm. Let me parse: "Its `verb` is a word that is no verb here, or an auxiliary while the main verb stands elsewhere." So the verb key holds (a) a non-verb word, or (b) an auxiliary word, while the main verb stands elsewhere. Here verb="adding" — a word that is... "adding" is a verb form, so (a) no. (b) no.

But is "needs" as auxiliary a fault? Rule 2: "The verb of each clause, or that it has none. Its auxiliary and negation words." must be right. Here the auxiliary word "needs" is not an auxiliary; the verb is "needs". Words of one written clause held... hmm.

I think this is a real error: the main verb "needs" is held in the auxiliary slot, so no clause has "needs" as verb. That matches L5? "A clause of the message is not written: its verb is held as a modifier, a dependent, a head or a discourse word, and no clause has it as verb." — auxiliary is not in that list.

Hmm. Compare how the alt would write it. Let me consider a more common-sense grade: L8 (acceptable). The next layer sees "auxiliary=needs, verb=adding" and can figure out from context that Hannah needs to be added. Actually the next layer is told to decide meaning with context; the circuit says Hannah + needs + adding. Both words are in the right clause, in the right order. The statement "adding" is the verb of the clause with subject Hannah — that's arguably a wrong statement about who acts.

Similarly row 94? Let me think about consistency: For "we've got a new designer" they used aux='ve verb=got — correct. For "Hannah needs adding" they used aux=needs verb=adding — that treats a gerund complement as the main verb. Since a definite wrong statement is made about the clause's verb (the main verb "needs" demoted to auxiliary and the gerund "adding" made the verb of a declarative clause claiming Hannah adds), I'd call it L1-ish. The L1 rule text "an auxiliary while the main verb stands elsewhere" is about the reverse direction.

Honestly, cases like this are exactly "an auxiliary word is held in another place" — the rules mention "An `auxiliary` or `negation` word is held in another place, or negates the wrong clause" as L1. Here a non-auxiliary word is held in the auxiliary place — symmetric-ish, and the verb slot holds the wrong word. I'll grade L1? Hmm, risk.

Let me look at the alt for row 34 to see the other formalizer's view. Let me fetch alt for a few rows I'm unsure about: n=99 (row 34), n=8, etc. I'll fetch alts for n=99 and maybe n=59... Let me gather alts for uncertain rows in one call later.

Row 35 (n=100): "one more person, Viktor" — like row 29. L8.

Row 36 (n=101): "add my plumber, Gary" — L8.

Row 37 (n=107): "list Lee as Dr. Lee from now on" — like row 33/9. L8.

Row 38 (n=108): "I'd like Priya renamed to Priya S."
sop: c1 declarative 'd like subject I; c2 nonfinite verb=renamed subject=n2(Priya); r1 marker=to from c2 to n3 ("Priya S": dep Priya head S); r2 c1→c2. Good. L8.

Row 39 (n=109): "edit the person Mihai so the name reads Mihai Popa"
sop: c1 imperative edit complement=n1(the person); n2 Mihai; r1 marker=so from c1 to n2; n3 the name; c2 declarative verb=reads subject=n3 complement=n4; n4 "Mihai Popa" (dep Mihai head Popa); r2 from n1 to n2.

Problems: r1 marker=so from c1 to n2 (Mihai) — "so" introduces the clause "the name reads Mihai Popa", not "Mihai". Wrong end → L3. And c2 is untied (L6). Yes: "so" relation should be c1→c2.

Grade L3. Quote: 'so the name reads Mihai Popa'. Correction: r1 from c1 to c2 marker="so", and r2 from n1 to n2 (apposition) fine.

Row 40 (n=111): "Priya got married last month, so her name should be Priya Shah now"
sop: c1 declarative aux=got verb=married subject=Priya complement=n2(last month); k1 so c1 c2; c2 declarative aux=should verb=be modifier=now subject=n3(her name) complement=n4.

Hmm: "should be" — verb "be" with auxiliary "should": settled case "A form of 'be' that is the only verb of its clause is the verb." Fine. L8.

Row 41 (n=113): "I spelled Tom wrong, it's actually Thom - would you fix that?"
sop: c1 declarative spelled modifier=wrong subject I complement Tom; c2 declarative verb="'s" modifier=actually subject=it complement=Thom; c3 interrogative would fix subject you complement that; k1 coordination c1 c3; r1 from c3 to c2.

Issues: k1 joins c1 and c3 but "it's actually Thom" (c2) stands between them — "A coordination with a clause between two of its conjuncts that belongs to none of them fails: L3." Here c2 belongs to none of the conjuncts (it's tied to c3 by r1). So k1 (c1, c3) has c2 in between → L3.

Hmm, but "the earlier wire a coordination joins is the wire that ends right before the conjunction, or a wire that holds it". Here the semicolon/dash... The message: "I spelled Tom wrong, it's actually Thom - would you fix that?" The clause "it's actually Thom" is between "I spelled Tom wrong" and "would you fix that". The coordination k1 joins c1 and c3 across c2 → fails per the settled case. And per that case, the coordination should join c2 and c3 (or c1 and c2).

Also "wrong" as modifier — fine.

Also c2's verb is "'s" — "it's actually Thom" — verb "'s" (is) as verb: settled case allows "be" as verb. Fine.

Grade L3. Quote: 'it's actually Thom - would you fix that'. Note: the coordination joins "I spelled Tom wrong" with the question across the clause "it's actually Thom". Correction: k1 conjunct=$c2 conjunct=$c3 (or coordination of c1,c2 and then...). Simplest: k1 conjunction none? The message joins by "," and "-". Let's write:

@n1 nominal head="I"
@c1 declarative verb="spelled" modifier="wrong" subject=$n1 complement=$n2
@n2 nominal head="Tom"
@n3 nominal head="it"
@c2 declarative verb="'s" modifier="actually" subject=$n3 complement=$n4
@n4 nominal head="Thom"
@k1 coordination conjunct=$c1 conjunct=$c2
@n5 nominal head="you"
@n6 nominal head="that"
@c3 interrogative auxiliary="would" verb="fix" subject=$n5 complement=$n6
@r1 relation from=$c2 to=$c3

All words covered: I spelled Tom wrong it 's actually Thom would you fix that. Yes.

Row 42 (n=114): "rename Mihai to Mihai B. and add him to the weekly review" — good. L8.

Row 43 (n=115): "when I search for Ana I get confused with the client; can we change our Ana to Ana (design)?"
sop: r1 marker=when from c2 to c1; c1 declarative search subject I; r2 marker=for from c1 to n2(Ana); c2 declarative aux=get verb=confused subject=I; r3 marker=with from c2 to n4(client); c3 interrogative can change subject we complement n6(our Ana); r4 marker=to from c3 to n7(Ana); n8 "design"; k1 coordination c2 c3; r5 from n7 to n8.
All words: "when"(marker) "I" n1 "search" "for" "Ana" n2 "I" n3 "get" "confused" "with" "the client" n4 ";" "can we change our Ana to Ana (design)" n6="our Ana", n7="Ana", n8="design", r5 apposition. Good. L8.

Row 44 (n=117): "Mihai -> Michael" — n1 nominal dep Mihai dep ">" head Michael; c1 fragment complement n1. Acceptable (fragment, arrow as dependent). L8.

Row 45 (n=123): "Mihai, rename to Mihai Dan" — good, but note "Mihai" n1 is complement of c1 and r1 marker=to from c1 to n2. Fine. L8.

Row 46 (n=127): "get rid of the person called Tom" — c1 imperative aux=get verb=rid, r1 of from c1 to n1; c2 nonfinite called complement Tom, r2 from n1 to c2. Good. L8.

Now, uncertain ones: row 18 (n=60) L1 clear. Row 19 (n=62) L1 clear. Row 23 (n=72) L3. Row 39 (n=109) L3. Row 41 (n=113) L3. Row 34 (n=99) uncertain — let me fetch alt.

Let me get alt for n=99 and also revisit n=8 (already judged L8).

I'll fetch alt for row 34 only for now (cheap), and decide.

Actually the alt won't settle the rules question, but it might indicate a sensible reading. Let's look.

content.text:
n=72: alt uses k1 coordination with conjunction "so" — good; so alt is right → use as corrected sop.

n=99: alt writes "needs" as verb of c1, "adding" as nonfinite clause tied to c1. That's the right reading. So the sop's aux=needs/verb=adding is a wrong statement. Grade: L1 ("Its verb is a word that is no verb here, or an auxiliary while the main verb stands elsewhere" — here the main verb "needs" stands in the auxiliary slot, and the gerund occupies the verb slot of a declarative clause claiming Hannah adds). I'll grade L1 with note quoting 'Hannah needs adding', and use alt as the corrected sop.

Hmm, is L1 vs L8 fair? Let me consider the "next layer" test again: circuit says one clause, aux "needs", verb "adding", subject Hannah. "Hannah needs adding" — the next layer would interpret the aspect/aux wrongly; "needs" is the main verb and not an auxiliary. The rule set says aux words must be right; a non-auxiliary word held as an auxiliary with the main verb displaced is the same kind of fault L1 names ("an auxiliary while the main verb stands elsewhere" — the mirror). I'll go L1.

n=109: alt writes k1 "so" joining c1 and c2, with "Mihai" as a dependent of "person". So alt is right → use as correction. Note: alt holds "Mihai" as dependent of "the person" nominal — allowed by the case "A number or a name right after a noun ... may be a dependent in that noun's nominal, or a nominal of its own tied to the noun". Good.

n=113: alt: n2 head="Tom wrong" — hmm, "Tom wrong" as head of a nominal — is that OK? Words "Tom wrong" in one head is odd but a multi-word head is allowed for names ("Team lunch"). Hmm, "Tom wrong" — the rule "A name of several words may stand whole in head". "Tom wrong" isn't a name.
